title: Formation of Andhra Pradesh and Early State Politics

concepts.partName: Andhra Rashtra Nirmanam (Formation of Andhra State)
concepts.bodyMd:
Potti Sriramulu began a fast unto death in Madras city on **19 October 1952**, demanding a separate Andhra state. After a 58-day continuous fast, Sriramulu died — his self-sacrifice set the Andhra region ablaze with anger.

Coastal Andhra, Rayalaseema, and the Telangana-adjacent border areas erupted in unrest: processions, demonstrations, public meetings, and student agitation broke out everywhere. Wherever there were Telugus, that unrest was felt.

With this pressure, the government's hand was forced. On **1 October 1953** PM Nehru announced in Parliament that an Andhra state would be formed with undisputed districts.

### The Contest for Andhra Congress Legislature Party Leadership

At the time Andhra state was being formed, the number of elected Congress representatives from the Andhra region was comparatively small. Ranga's Kisan Mazdoor Praja Party and Prakasam's Praja Party had split Congress's strength, and the Communists too stood as a united rival bloc. In this situation, Andhra Congress needed to elect a legislature party leader.

*   **Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy** contested for this post.
*   The then minister **Shankar Reddy**'s name was proposed by minister **Pattabhirama Rao**; it was also rumoured that Rajaji campaigned for Shankar Reddy.
*   Once nominations closed, sentiment reversed in Srikakulam, Visakhapatnam, and East Godavari district circles.
*   On **Gopala Reddi**'s advice, Shankar Reddy withdrew from the race.
*   Sanjeeva Reddy accepted both the state Congress presidency and the leadership of the Congress Legislature Party.

### The Capital City Debate

Deciding the capital of the new Andhra state proved contentious, with three parties each pushing rival cities.

*   **Visakhapatnam** was too distant for Rayalaseema.
*   The **Kisan Mazdoor Lok Party** first proposed Tirupati, but Prakasam disliked Tirupati.
*   Sanjeeva Reddy's own home town, Anantapur, was unacceptable to others as he himself knew.
*   Rajaji's name being attached to a proposal made some hold a grudge, so Nellore too was dropped.
*   The remaining choice was **Kurnool**, which all three parties eventually accepted.

Even so, when the Andhra formation bill came up for debate in the Madras legislature, the Communists — weak in Rayalaseema — proposed keeping Kurnool only as a temporary name while shifting the real capital to Vijayawada. The Kisan Lok Party pushed for Tirupati instead, seen by critics as an attempt to build KLP's own strength there.

With five non-Andhra members voting in Kurnool's favour, neither the Vijayawada nor the Tirupati proposal secured enough votes. The arrangement collapsed back to Kurnool.

### The First Andhra Ministry — T. Prakasam (1953–54)

When Andhra state was carved out of Madras, the 140-seat assembly's party strength stood as:

| Party | Seats |
|---|---|
| Congress | 51 |
| Communists | 43 |
| Krishikar Lok Party | 14 |
| Praja Party | 6 |
| Praja Socialist Party | 15 |
| Scheduled Caste Federation | 2 |
| Independents | 9 |

Congress lacked a full majority and could not form a government without other parties' support. On top of this, even Nehru was said to be against a Prakasam-led ministry, and critics called a Prakasam ministry "a headless torso." Sanjeeva Reddy and **Alluri Satyanarayana Raju**, using their full political skill, brought Prakasam back into the Congress fold.

PM Nehru inaugurated Andhra state on **1 October 1953**. Prakasam became Chief Minister, with the following ministry:

| Minister | Portfolio/Position |
|---|---|
| T. Prakasam | Chief Minister |
| Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy | Deputy Chief Minister |
| Tenneti Viswanatham | Minister |
| S.B.P. Pattabhirama Rao | Minister |
| Sanjeevayya | Minister |
| Kadapa Kotireddy | Minister |

Uniquely in the history of parliamentary parties, Prakasam was Chief Minister without being party leader. Since Tenneti did not leave the Praja Party, Andhra's first government was, from the outset, a mixed/coalition government. Later Gouthu Latchanna too was brought in, making it a three-party mix.

Four ministry members were from Rayalaseema. The assembly's real working strength was only around 70–75, making the government inherently unstable.

The government appointed the Shanti Ramamurthy Committee to look into prohibition, and the committee recommended lifting the ban. Congress's own ideology opposed implementing this recommendation, and a no-confidence motion was brought against the government. Congress members Shankar Reddy and Adusumilli Subrahmanyam ended up voting against their own government, and the Prakasam ministry fell by a single vote on **6 November 1954**, bringing the state under Governor's rule.

Around the same time, Rajaji's new education scheme created a storm in the Madras assembly, but Tamil members did not press for his resignation. Telugu leaders, in this period, proved unable to hold ministries stable — the state remained under President's/Governor's rule for about sixteen months.

### The Gopala Reddi Ministry and the 1955 Elections

With Governor's rule from December 1954, mid-term elections were held in **1955**. Remembering their 1952 defeat, Congress and former Congress members prepared cautiously in advance. To counter the Communists, Congress formed a **United Front** with the Praja Party and the Kisan Lok Party.

Delimitation increased the assembly's seats from 140 to 194, and Communists, anticipating power, entered the contest with major preparation.

The 1955 elections were seen as a special referendum for Andhra to avoid repeating the "Communist mistake." A great movement arose to safeguard democracy in the state, winning huge public support — described as a "people's victory." What swung the middle classes to vote overwhelmingly for Congress was concern over "certain issues, not certain leaders" — a zealous desire to protect democracy and back a national party. Congress achieved a decisive win, and state-level leaders again came to the fore.

**Election results (1955):**

| Party | Contested | Won |
|---|---|---|
| Congress | 196 | 146 |
| Communists | 169 | 15 |
| Praja Socialist Party | 45 | 13 |
| Independents | 1,692 | 22 |

Of 13 contesting ministers, Tenneti Viswanatham and Shankar Reddy lost. Kurnool, which Congress had won in 1952, went to the Communists this time. Communist stalwarts Makineni Basavapunnayya, Tarimela Nagi Reddy, Moturi Hanumantha Rao, and Chandra Rajeshwara Rao, along with many others, also lost. Prakasam won — at 86 years of age.

The question of leadership arose again. Gopala Reddi, among the senior leaders, stood for it. Sanjeeva Reddy, mindful of state-building responsibilities and of having earlier been crowned deputy under Prakasam, did not press his own claim too far. Delhi's Congress leadership decided on **Gopala Reddi** as leader, and Sanjeeva Reddy agreed to remain as Deputy CM.

**United Front Ministry (1955):**

| Minister | Position |
|---|---|
| Bezwada Gopala Reddi | Chief Minister |
| Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy | Deputy Chief Minister |
| Kalluri Chandramouli | Minister |
| Kala Venkatrao | Minister |
| Gouthu Latchanna | Minister |
| A.B. Nageswara Rao | Minister |
| Oblu Reddy | Minister |
| D. Sanjeevayya | Minister |
| Neerukonda Ramarao | Minister (Food) |

Neerukonda Ramarao, who had taken oath as Food Minister, died on **4 May 1955** at the age of 41. With Gopala Reddi as CM, Alluri Satyanarayana Raju became PCC president.

It must be said that after the 1955 elections, the era of the "old-guard generation" ended in Andhra. Prakasam, due to old age, did not contest for leadership and himself showed little interest in the matter. Dr. Pattabhi Sitaramayya became Governor of Madhya Pradesh and left state politics. Acharya Ranga, who contested for state Congress president and lost, remained a lone figure thereafter, surviving in memory only as "the farmers' friend."

### Kurnool as the Capital City

Kurnool's population at the time was only **40,000**. The Collector's office was converted into the Secretariat, and the Collector's office itself was shifted to Nandyal. The Assembly was housed in the District Court building, and Governor Trivedi brought 4,000 tents from Delhi.

The Collector's residence became the Chief Secretary B. Pullareddy's residence. Even so, department heads and directorate offices could not be accommodated conveniently in Kurnool. Until Hyderabad became the AP capital, these offices continued to function out of Madras city itself.

On cabinet meeting days, department heads travelled from Madras by train, alighting at Guntakal and being driven onward to Kurnool by car. The Executive Engineer's residence on the K.C. Canal bank was converted into Raj Bhavan.

With Prakasam's encouragement, a 45-day budget session of the assembly was held in Visakhapatnam. Tikkavarapu Ramireddy Hall, a university hostel, was converted into the assembly hall, and legislators were lodged in university hostels. At this Vizag session itself, the bill for Venkateswara University was approved, and primary education was nationalized.

Governor Trivedi worked with great personal dedication on the question of Andhra's new capital, working through the night with engineers so the work would not stall — down to arranging the water-supply pipes needed for the roads of the town destined to become the state capital.

* * *

Before Andhra Pradesh was formed, an agreement was reached in **1956** between the leaders of the Telangana and Andhra regions, known as the **Peddamanushula Oppandam (Gentlemen's Agreement)**.

**Signatories:**

| From Andhra | From Telangana |
|---|---|
| Bezwada Gopala Reddi (CM) | Dr. Burgula Ramakrishna Rao (CM) |
| Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy | Konda Venkata Ranga Reddy |
| Alluri Satyanarayana Raju | J.V. Narsingarao |
| Gouthu Latchanna | Dr. Marri Chenna Reddy |

### Terms of the Agreement

1.  Central and general administrative expenditure to be borne proportionately between the Andhra and Telangana regions; Telangana's surplus reserved for that region's own development. This arrangement to last five years, after which Telangana's legislature members could ask for a further five years.
2.  Prohibition to be implemented in Telangana as decided by Telangana's own legislature members.
3.  Higher educational facilities in Telangana reserved for Telangana students and to be further developed; all technical and other educational institutions in the state to reserve admissions proportionately for Telangana students.
4.  If unification required reducing certain jobs, the reduction to happen proportionately.
5.  Recruitment to government jobs to be based on the population ratio of the two regions.
6.  For five years, Urdu to retain its existing position in Telangana's administration and courts; regional bodies could later review this. No prior knowledge of Telugu to be a precondition for joining service, though a rule could require learning it within two years of appointment.
7.  Candidates for posts reserved for Telangana to have twelve years' residence in the region.
8.  A **Regional Committee** to be set up for the all-round development of Telangana.
9.  Sale of agricultural land in Telangana to be under the control of the Regional Committee.
10.  The Regional Committee would have 20 members — two elected MLAs from each of Telangana's nine districts, plus six members chosen from Telangana representatives in Parliament or the state legislature.
11.  All Telangana ministers except the Chief Minister and Speaker to be members of the Regional Committee.
12.  The Regional Committee to be constituted under Article 371 of the Constitution and appointed by the Governor.
13.  Though not a statutory body, the Regional Committee would deliberate on procedure, development, irrigation and other agricultural schemes, industrial development, Telangana employment, public health, and prohibition.
14.  Disagreements between the state government and the Regional Committee to be referred to the Government of India.
15.  In the absence of a fresh agreement, the arrangement to be reviewed after ten years.
16.  Cabinet composition to follow an Andhra:Telangana ratio of **6:4**, with one Muslim minister from Telangana.
17.  If the Chief Minister is from Andhra, the Deputy Chief Minister must be from Telangana, and vice versa. Of the Home, Finance, Planning, Development, Commerce, and Industries portfolios, at least two must go to Telangana.
18.  Hyderabad's Pradesh Congress leaders sought a separate Congress committee for Telangana until 1962; Andhra Congress leaders raised no objection to this.

The same "Peddamanushulu" met again on **14 August 1956** and finalised further points in a joint note. The new state's name was to be "Andhra-Telangana," as Telangana representatives wished, and this appeared in the draft bill — but the Joint Select Committee changed it to "**Andhra Pradesh**," as Andhra representatives had wanted. On the High Court, Telangana representatives wanted the main bench to remain in Hyderabad with a branch at Guntur, while Andhra representatives wanted the entire High Court to stay in Hyderabad.

### Telangana Safeguards

**Regional Standing Body**

1.  Andhra Pradesh to have a single joint legislature for the whole state, one Governor, and a Council of Ministers responsible to that legislature.
2.  For certain special matters, Telangana would be treated administratively as one region.
3.  Telangana to have its own Standing Committee, comprising Telangana's ministers and legislature members; the Chief Minister would not be a member of it.
4.  Legislative matters on specific subjects to be referred to this Committee; it could also make proposals on general financial matters (excluding routine or emergency expenditure).
5.  The Committee's advice would normally be accepted by government and legislature; disagreements to go to the Governor, whose decision would be final.

**Subjects entrusted to the Regional Committee:**

1.  Development and economic planning within schemes framed by the legislature
2.  Local administration — municipal corporations, constitutional powers, development trusts, district boards, village administration bodies
3.  Public health, sanitation, local hospitals and treatment centres
4.  Primary and secondary education
5.  Admissions to Telangana's educational institutions
6.  Prohibition
7.  Sale of agricultural land
8.  Cottage and small-scale industries
9.  Agricultural cooperative societies, markets/fairs

### Residence Rules and Employee Retrenchment

Recruitment to posts reserved for Telangana was to treat the region as a single unit, filled according to the domicile rules then in force under Hyderabad regulations. The Government of India was to advise the state government on measures needed to preserve Urdu's position in the existing administrative and judicial system.

On retrenchment, the Government of India did not intend that serving employees should be removed unless unification made it necessary. Even then, without any deliberate scheme, the aim was to absorb Hyderabad state employees into the wider Andhra Pradesh service as far as possible. Any necessary retrenchment was to be applied uniformly across the enlarged state's employees.

Deciding expenditure based on the state's financial needs remained a matter for the state government and legislature. But the Government of India accepted the principle of proportionate sharing of central/general administrative expenditure and dedicating Telangana's surplus to Telangana's development, as agreed by both regions' representatives — and wanted this specifically brought to the notice of the Andhra Chief Minister. This letter carried the signature of Hyderabad Chief Minister Dr. Burgula Ramakrishna Rao, dated **14 August 1956** — the day the Hyderabad government was itself dissolved.

### Fate of the Agreement's Provisions

*   Points 2, 3, 7, 8, 10, and 11 of the agreement were incorporated into the Andhra Pradesh Regional Committee Order.
*   Point 9 was incorporated into Article 371 of the Constitution.
*   Safeguard points 9 and 6 were incorporated into the Andhra Pradesh Regional Committee Order, 1956.
*   Point 6-B, on Domestic Rules of State Government (state employment rules), was incorporated into the Regional Committee Order, 1958.
*   The remaining points were never formally recognised as part of the "Gentlemen's Agreement."

Union Home Minister **Govind Ballabh Pant** directed leaders on both sides to obtain a legal expert's advice on which points were constitutionally valid, and to finalise the matter on that basis. This task was left to Telangana's leaders while Andhra's leaders departed for Kurnool.

The bill was introduced in Parliament by Pant as the "Andhra-Telangana Pradesh Bill," but on a member's suggestion the name "Andhra Pradesh" was adopted instead. Andhra High Court Chief Justice Koka Subba Rao suggested to Rangareddy that Hyderabad's High Court alone be retained. Rangareddy, familiar with Urdu-speaking judges, accepted this advice, and the Andhra and Telangana High Courts merged into one.

In April 1955, the bill (with some amendments) was placed before the Kurnool legislature: the new state's name would be **Andhra Pradesh**, with capital and High Court at Hyderabad. The 1957 elections would apply only to Telangana, with elections across the whole of Andhra Pradesh only in 1962, and the upper house would have 72 members, with some amendments. On **13 April 1956**, the Hyderabad legislature approved this bill, and it received presidential assent on **31 August**.

Andhra Pradesh's legislature strength was fixed at 301. At the time of formation, Andhra's own legislature had 196 members, and Telangana's members in the Hyderabad legislature numbered 101 — giving a combined total of **297** with which the Andhra Pradesh legislature began.

* * *

concepts.partName: Andhra Pradesh Avatarana (The Birth of Andhra Pradesh)
concepts.bodyMd:
PM Nehru inaugurated the new state of Andhra Pradesh on **1 November 1956**.

### The Contest for Chief Ministership

The question of who would lead the new ministry arose immediately. Though Prakasam again wished to lead, for many reasons this was not universally acceptable, and by then, being very old, he himself showed little interest. From the Andhra side, Bezwada Gopala Reddi and Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy entered the contest, but both declared they would step aside if Burgula Ramakrishna Rao were made leader. Dr. Marri Chenna Reddy, though not entirely opposed to Ramakrishna Rao, pledged to contest so that Ramakrishna Rao would not be elected unopposed.

With Telangana emerging as a fresh political force of nine districts, its swing mattered greatly. Telangana's leader was **Konda Venkat Ranga Reddy**, whose followers included Marri Chenna Reddy and the Velama leader J.V. Narsingarao. Within Telangana, two factions existed:

*   **Telangana-vadulu**, led by Konda Venkat Ranga Reddy
*   **Vishalandhra-vadulu**, prominent among them Valluri Basavaraju — a capital-city politician without Ranga Reddy's grassroots strength in Telangana's villages

All Andhra and Telangana members gathered at Kurnool, and Congress observer **Shriman Narayan** came from the high command to oversee proceedings. Ranga Reddy, unwell, did not attend. Chenna Reddy went in with his own supporters, while Narsingarao's and Ramakrishna Rao's groups voted for **Sanjeeva Reddy**, who was elected AP Congress Legislature Party leader and became the first Chief Minister of united Andhra Pradesh.

Gopala Reddi, though a contestant, immediately joined Sanjeeva Reddy's ministry. Ramakrishna Rao, who had helped, accepted the post of Kerala Governor and withdrew from AP politics. Chenna Reddy, who had opposed, alone remained without a post.

**Sanjeeva Reddy's first AP ministry (Telangana members):** Konda Venkat Ranga Reddy, V.B. Raju, J.V. Narsingarao, Mahdi Nawaz Jung, and Mandumula Narsingarao. As per the Gentlemen's Agreement, ministry posts were to be shared between Andhra and Telangana proportionately, but of Telangana's several factions, only five ministerial posts were given in total. Nookala Ramachandra Reddy, who deserved a sixth post, was instead given the position of Pradesh Congress Secretary.

In this stronghold of Telangana politics, Neelam and Alluri worked their political strategy skilfully, outmanoeuvring the Vishalandhra advocates while dividing the Telangana camp. Per the Gentlemen's Agreement, the Deputy Chief Minister's post was to go to a Telangana leader, but it was left unassigned for a time. This exploited the mutual rivalries among Telangana's own leaders and became an early sign of Andhra–Telangana disunity.

Telangana's demand for separate development for itself was not unreasonable, but concrete action lagged. Rayalaseema representative Sanjeeva Reddy, drawing on his own region's experience under the earlier **Sri Bagh** agreement (which was similarly not implemented), came to treat the Telangana Gentlemen's Agreement as similarly unnecessary to honour, with the Neelam–Alluri leadership acting in unison throughout. Even though the Marathwada and Karnataka regions had separated from the old Hyderabad state, the larger Andhra Pradesh — comparatively bigger than those regions — still received Hyderabad as its capital.

### Nehru's Gandhi Bhavan Speech and Composite Culture

Soon after arriving in Hyderabad, PM Nehru addressed Congress legislators and workers at Gandhi Bhavan. He described Hyderabad's transformation as one of the greatest changes on India's map since independence — not merely political but psychological, since a princely state had vanished from the map. The Hyderabad state had been split into three regions, one of which merged into Andhra state, marking a great national transformation.

On **composite culture**, Nehru observed that Hyderabad's people had developed a distinctive culture with both good and less desirable elements. Old "durbari" traditions unsuited to modern India needed gradual replacement, he said, but he stressed that Hyderabad's genuinely good elements, its composite culture, should not be discarded for anyone's convenience, and that this would ultimately benefit Andhras too. He said Telangana should have a prominent place within Andhra Pradesh, and that both regions must accommodate each other with tolerance and goodwill, neither harming the other.

At the historic inauguration at **L.B. Stadium**, Nehru spoke in Hindustani, which the coastal and Rayalaseema audience did not understand. Ramakrishna Rao translated it into Telugu, easing the unrest in the gathering. His subsequent departure from the state left behind an impression of a divide between the two regions, making mutual understanding difficult.

Hyderabad — a city of about 96 square miles, with fine government buildings, High Court, general hospitals, and assembly building — became the Andhra capital. Telangana's industries — Sirpur Paper Mills, Sirsilk, Bodhan Sugar Factory, Singareni collieries, Bellampalli coal mines, Praga Tools, and the Secunderabad railway workshop — were significant not just in India but across Asia. Shifting the capital away from Madras brought real hardships and struggles that were personally experienced.

### Administrative Friction: "Andhra Procedure" vs "Telangana Procedure"

Andhra people, mainly in Telangana, hoped that with their long-cherished Vishalandhra achieved, Andhra language and culture — long suppressed — would flourish. They hoped that the vast coastal region, Krishna–Godavari waters, Telangana's industrial resources, and Rayalaseema's minerals combined would bring prosperity through planned, unified development.

Once Sanjeeva Reddy settled in as CM, for about a year, staff transfers and paperwork dominated. Laws and rules from the two erstwhile administrations were never properly harmonised, and "Andhra–Telangana" distinctions grew more entrenched in government rather than less.

Because Telangana was treated merely as "attached" to Andhra, officialdom held that the whole administration should follow "Andhra procedure" — essentially Madras procedure, popularly called "Boston Home" procedure — with no need to consider "Telangana procedure." Hyderabad had earlier followed the "Bombay pattern," and the two systems were fundamentally incompatible.

Copies of the "Boston Home" procedure manual were not even available in print, and Telangana staff had no familiarity with it at all. Kurnool officials pushed ahead with implementation regardless. Telangana employees felt shut out of jobs "from the Governor downward," with the middle rungs of Telangana employment unable to secure a foothold.

There was no sense of shared purpose from the outset. Kurnool's high-handedness was resented in Hyderabad, and Hyderabad's grievances found no hearing in Kurnool.

### Sanjeeva Reddy's First Term and the Neelam–Alluri Rivalry

In **1957**, assembly elections were held only for the Telangana region, since the Hyderabad Provincial Congress Committee — as per the Gentlemen's Agreement — remained separate until 1962. This was intended to shield Telangana Congress leaders' influence in candidate selection from Andhra Congress leaders' pressure. After the 1957 elections, the question of merging the still-separate Hyderabad Provincial Congress with the Andhra Provincial Congress arose. The high command advised a single unified state Congress, and the Hyderabad committee accepted.

After 1957, Sanjeeva Reddy again became CM. A Legislative Council was formed the same year. As CM, Sanjeeva Reddy grew stronger while his deputy Alluri consolidated his hold as PCC president.

But when AICC president **U.N. Dhebar** appointed Alluri as his secretary, new turbulence began in Andhra politics. From here, the **Neelam–Alluri rivalry** took centre stage. Sanjeeva Reddy's administration lasted three years and two months, after which he went to Delhi as AICC president.

Satyanarayana Raju's own ambition to become CM was not unreasonable. He was an attractive, capable, and skilled campaigner who knew Hindi well and had translated Rahul Sankrityayan's _Volga se Ganga_ into Telugu. "Truth" (Satyam) had been Sanjeeva Reddy's own watchword, yet his trusted associate turned against that very ideal, and enmity grew between former friends.

A.C. Subba Reddy also nursed ambitions for the CM post, encouraged by friends. Sanjeeva Reddy watched these moves closely, while Alluri worked to crush them and tried instead to bring Kerala Governor Ramakrishna Rao into contention.

Dhebar had consulted both sides in advance. Sanjeeva Reddy and Gopala Reddi were initially not contestants; Ramakrishna Rao clearly refused to re-enter state politics; Gopala Reddi showed no enthusiasm either. The view emerged that Satyanarayana Raju, lacking administrative experience, was fine as a minister but unsuited to be CM. Eventually his own side brought Sanjeevayya and Pattabhirama Rao into active campaigning.

In the end, Sanjeeva Reddy's opponents got their one moment of triumph — they backed Alluri for CM. Alluri, unable to take the post himself, agreed instead to **D. Sanjeevayya** as CM, becoming the chief architect behind that choice.

Though Sanjeeva Reddy had accepted the AICC presidency, his focus stayed fixed on state politics, feeling that post to matter less to him than leading the state legislature party. Congress rules barred organisational office-holders from also holding legislature posts. Alluri, after his term, did not seek Rajya Sabha membership, but Sanjeeva Reddy himself remained an AP Legislative Assembly member from Kalahasti until the end.

### Damodaram Sanjeevayya as Chief Minister

**D. Sanjeevayya** took oath as AP's second Chief Minister on **10 January 1960**, at the age of 38 — the state's first Harijan Chief Minister. His ministry formation appeared straightforward: four expected persons became ministers, Telangana's senior leader Konda Venkat Ranga Reddy received the Deputy CM post, and another Telangana leader, **Nookala Narottama Reddy**, became PCC president.

Narottama Reddy's unanimous election as PCC president stirred fresh discontent in Telangana's districts. It fed the criticism against Alluri that just as Rayalaseema leaders had once been favoured unfairly, Alluri was now favouring Telangana leaders selectively for his own ends while curbing others' opportunities.

After Nookala Ramachandra Reddy became a minister, questions arose over why his brother Narottama Reddy also needed the PCC post, and accusations spread that Alluri was repeating Sanjeeva Reddy's earlier mistakes in a new form. Caught in this conflict, Narottama Reddy had to resign as PCC president, and both sides settled on **Mallipudi Pallam Raju** as the new Congress president.

As Alluri's missteps mounted, Sanjeevayya grew stronger and increasingly independent of him, and disagreement grew between the two. Sanjeevayya was self-made, born into a Harijan family, having endured great hardship before reaching prominence. His rise was one many attributed to Rajaji's early patronage, and Rajaji, Prakasam, Gopala Reddi, and Sanjeeva Reddy had each shown patience toward him while he served as minister under them.

Once Sanjeevayya rose, however, his rivals began scheming against him from the start. Before assembly elections he declared his own intention to contest for the CM post, setting the stage for the high command's intervention.

### Sanjeeva Reddy's Return and Resignation

Though Sanjeeva Reddy still had eight months left as AICC president and could have sought re-election, the high command showed no inclination to retain him there. He pressed the urgency of the upcoming Prime Ministerial contest to justify his return to state politics, and built an atmosphere ensuring his unanimous election as AP Legislature Congress leader. Fresh candidates were fielded with the specific aim of making him CM again.

In the **1962 elections**, internal factionalism cost Congress around 50 seats, while the Communists won 51. In Telangana, Congress's strength fell sharply — from 68 seats won in 1957 to no more than 62 this time. In Communist strongholds like Khammam and Nalgonda, Congress's own campaigning backfired; in Warangal, its earlier 14 seats fell to no more than 7.

Even so, Congress won one seat in Khammam, two in Medak, and an additional three in Karimnagar, while losing one seat in Hyderabad and two in Adilabad. Notable losers included Deputy CM Konda Venkat Ranga Reddy, ministers Konda Lakshman Bapuji and Smt. Masuma Begum, former minister J.V. Narsingarao, Telangana Regional Development Committee chairman Achyuta Reddy, and Bommakanti Satyanarayana Rao. The Jana Sangh failed to win a single seat.

After 1962, **Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy** became CM for a second time. This time Dr. Marri Chenna Reddy finally found a place in the ministry, and the ministry was formed on a broader basis than before, though Alluri had no place in it, and neither did Sanjeevayya (who, not having become AICC president, bore no active grievance against the ministry at the time). The China war emergency had not yet arisen.

Alluri Satyanarayana Raju died on **2 September 1963**, after which AP politics briefly lacked the accustomed rivalry framing Sanjeeva Reddy's leadership. In 1964, the Communist Party split into two.

Kurnool district's bus routes were nationalised, and bus owners went to the Supreme Court and won. An expert committee had earlier ruled that Nellore, Chittoor, and Kadapa districts' routes should be nationalised before Kurnool's — a sequence not followed. Opposition leaders Pidatala Rangareddy and Vijayabhaskara Reddy's attacks on the CM over this were seen by some as personally motivated, but their complaints were upheld by the Supreme Court on **23 February 1964**. Taking the blame, Sanjeeva Reddy resigned as CM immediately after.

Jawaharlal Nehru died on **27 May 1964**; Lal Bahadur Shastri became Prime Minister.

### Brahmananda Reddy's Tenure

**Kasu Brahmananda Reddy** became CM on **29 February 1964**, retaining all of Sanjeeva Reddy's previous cabinet members except Sanjeeva Reddy himself, and initially made no departmental changes. Four months later, without Sanjeeva Reddy's consent, he inducted Thota Ramaswamy, Chenchu Ramanaidu, and Tanneti Veeraraghavulu into the ministry.

A pattern noted in the state's politics was that whenever a leader rose to national prominence, his local strength within the state correspondingly weakened, and Sanjeeva Reddy followed this pattern. A rival faction emerged around **A.C. Subba Reddy**, encouraged by his allies.

Once Subba Reddy was inducted into the ministry, his Nellore district rival Chenchu Ramanaidu also secured a ministerial post. This emboldened Subba Reddy to intensify factional politics, splitting the ministry into two camps that in turn shaped district-level leadership contests. In Telangana, the long-standing rift between Nookala Ramachandra Reddy and Marri Chenna Reddy meant that when Chenna Reddy (Sanjeeva Reddy's opponent) joined the Brahmananda Reddy faction, Nookala aligned with Sanjeeva Reddy's faction.

Lal Bahadur Shastri died suddenly in **January 1966**; within 19 months, Congress's parliamentary party again needed a new leader. Sanjeeva Reddy, present at Shastri's last rites, joined other chief ministers (without consulting Brahmananda Reddy) in backing and strengthening Indira Gandhi. He felt that not being consulted on the PM question signalled his own declining prominence, and from here began his thoughts of removing Brahmananda Reddy.

In the contest held on **19 January 1966**, Indira Gandhi defeated Morarji Desai to become Prime Minister. In the **1967 elections**, Congress lost in many states but retained a narrow majority (22 members) at the centre. Non-Congress governments were formed in Tamil Nadu, Punjab, Kerala, West Bengal, Orissa, Bihar, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, and the Union Territory of Delhi.

Agriculture and food ministers at both centre and state levels uniformly lost their seats. After the elections Indira Gandhi again became PM, Morarji Desai accepted the Deputy PM post, and Sanjeeva Reddy became Lok Sabha Speaker.

In the state, Congress won **164 seats**, and Brahmananda Reddy emerged unchallenged as leader. In the same period, Dr. Marri Chenna Reddy was inducted as a Union Minister at the centre — seen by some as the CM's deliberate move to keep Chenna Reddy away from state politics, and by others as V.B. Raju's own strategy with an eye on future state politics.

### Death of the Last Nizam

**Nizam Mir Usman Ali Khan**, who lived 89 years, died on **21 February 1967**. He ascended the throne in 1911, ruled Hyderabad state for 37 years, held the Raj Pramukh post for a time after accession, and, following Andhra Pradesh's formation, lived out his remaining years without state authority, dying as a private citizen. Indira Gandhi's condolence message called it "the end of an era" — a description genuinely apt in Telugu history.

Though Brahmananda Reddy wished otherwise, the ruling establishment blocked a Secunderabad Lok Sabha candidacy in the 1967 elections as punishment for having supported Morarji Desai in the PM contest. Dr. Burgula Ramakrishna Rao passed away on **15 September** — the man who had helped shape and envision the comprehensive form of Andhra Pradesh, who had served outside its borders as Kerala and then Uttar Pradesh Governor, dying in an unfulfilled dream, distant from both regions he had once led.

In **April 1968**, the Hyderabad High Court ruled against Chenna Reddy on his election petition, and he appealed to the Supreme Court. That year, the All India Congress annual sessions, held with great pomp in Hyderabad, won Brahmananda Reddy wide approval, securing him membership of the Congress Working Committee and national prominence by early 1968.

### Chenna Reddy's Political Trajectory

The Supreme Court eventually ruled against Chenna Reddy in the election petition, forcing his resignation from both his Union Minister post and Rajya Sabha membership. Some police evidence surfacing in his favour (with Brahmananda Reddy's reported help) suggested the case against him was weak, according to his trusted associates, though newspapers reported this help proved of no use to him.

Chenna Reddy — a man of intense ambition unable to bear political isolation — responded by raising the banner of a "Democratic Front" against Congress whenever circumstances turned against him. He remained, nonetheless, the one Telangana leader recognised everywhere as CM material without ever having actually become AP's chief minister, despite Telangana's 1956-era claim to the post rightfully belonging to him. A skilled orator and campaigner, he was given the chairmanship of the Road Transport Corporation as a face-saving honour whenever V.B. Raju's faction found itself in difficulty; he had first become a minister as early as 1952.

### Brahmananda Reddy's Resignation (1971)

After the Bangalore Congress session, CM Brahmananda Reddy announced a new ministry in **July 1969**, excluding Nookala Ramachandra Rao and Ramabhupala Reddy. With Nookala's exclusion, the Deputy CM post went to **J.V. Narsingarao**.

Facing numerous difficult tests and trials, Brahmananda Reddy steered the state firmly through the turbulent years of 1969–70 with skill, and his capability was widely credited as the reason Andhra Pradesh did not break apart during that period.

The promise made by the "Peddamanushulu" (Gentlemen's Agreement) went unfulfilled, creating conditions that threatened state stability. CM Brahmananda Reddy resigned on **24 September 1971** — a democratically formed government effectively overthrown through agitation and pressure rather than through law.

Brahmananda Reddy described his resignation as an unparalleled sacrifice for state unity, a framing Indira Gandhi echoed in her own statement, though in substance it amounted to his being eased out. Because he chose to resign rather than actively push for a preferred successor of his own, AP's legislature members had to accept whichever leader was selected in Delhi.

With Indira Gandhi consolidating full central authority and pursuing her vision of socialism and modern political methods, she moved to install new leadership loyal to her policies within Congress governments and party organisations across the states. She toppled long-standing established leaderships to varying degrees, and this happened in Andhra Pradesh as elsewhere: a person suited to her policies was made both AP Chief Minister and PCC president, just as Sukhadia was removed in Rajasthan and V.P. Naik in Maharashtra.

### The 1969 Presidential Election and the Congress Split

Independent India's most intense Presidential contest occurred in **1969**, between **V.V. Giri** and **Sanjeeva Reddy** — an election that triggered a historic split in the Congress party. President Dr. Zakir Hussain's death had made Vice President V.V. Giri the acting President.

A section of Congress opposed making Giri's acting presidency permanent. When the party's official effort to field its own candidate failed, Indira Gandhi supported Giri's resignation as acting President and his contest as an independent candidate. When the Congress Parliamentary Party leadership issued a whip directing MPs to vote for the party's official candidate, Indira Gandhi disregarded it, instead advocating a "conscience vote" — openly signalling rebellion.

The Jana Sangh, Swatantra Party, the BKD, and nearly every other major party and faction decided to back Giri, blurring party lines in a contest fought almost entirely on ideological grounds. V.V. Giri won not through first-preference votes but through second-preference votes alone. In the Presidential election, **Andhra Pradesh gave Giri more votes than any other state**.
